paragraphs.text: Autosomal recessive intellectual developmental disorder-43 (MRT43) is an intellectual disability disorder caused by defects in WASHC4 (SWIP), a member of the WASH complex. The WASH complex is involved in actin polymerization and endosomal transport. The disorder was first reported as nonsyndromic intellectual disability (Ropers et al., 2011). Later reports described a broader, variable phenotype. Features can include short stature, macrocephaly or microcephaly, dysmorphic features, skeletal anomalies, motor dysfunction, and skeletal muscle involvement (Assoum et al., 2020; Courtland et al., 2021; Gangfuss et al., 2022).

paragraphs.text: Assoum et al. (2020) reported 3 patients from 2 unrelated families with syndromic intellectual disability. In the first family, 2 sisters aged 4 and 5.5 years had learning disabilities, macrocephaly, dysmorphic features, skeletal anomalies, and subependymal heterotopic nodules. The younger sister also had congenital absence of the right internal carotid artery and bilateral sensorineural hearing loss. The third patient was 34 years old and had mild intellectual disability, short stature, and microcephaly. Assoum et al. (2020) concluded that the phenotype associated with KIAA1033 is heterogeneous.

paragraphs.text: Courtland et al. (2021) retrospectively reviewed clinical findings from 7 children in Oman who were homozygous for the P1019R mutation; these were the patients originally reported by Ropers et al. (2011). Developmental delay or learning difficulties had been the main reason for medical evaluation. However, all patients also had motor symptoms (mean age, 10.4 years). Their movements were described as 'clumsy', with notable fine motor difficulties, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, and mild dysarthria on clinical examination. The patients were now an average of 21 years old, and their parents reported no notable worsening of symptoms.

paragraphs.text: In a large consanguineous family with autosomal recessive intellectual disability, Ropers et al. (2011) used homozygosity mapping, targeted exon enrichment, and high-throughput sequencing to identify a missense mutation in the SWIP gene. After SNP filtering, only 2 sequence changes remained. The SWIP change was considered causative based on high pathogenicity and conservation scores and on functional considerations. The mutation caused significantly reduced SWIP levels and destabilized the entire WASH complex. Courtland et al. (2021) identified this mutation as a homozygous c.3056C-G transversion in WASHC4, resulting in a pro1019-to-arg (P1019R) substitution.

paragraphs.text: Courtland et al. (2021) used CRISPR to create a mouse model carrying the human SWIP P1019R mutation. In brains of homozygous mutant mice, Strumpellin and WASH1 were markedly decreased (3.8% and 1.1% of wildtype, respectively). Spatial proteomics showed destabilization of the WASH complex, decreased abundance of an endosomal module, and increased abundance of a lysosomal module. Mutant cortical neurons had enlarged EEA1-positive early endosomes, as well as fewer but larger cathepsin D-positive puncta. At 7 months, motor cortex neurons of mutant mice showed lipofuscin accumulation. At 10 months, cleaved caspase-3 staining in the motor cortex was increased. Mutant mice had deficits in cued fear memory recall at both adolescence and adulthood. They also had motor deficits on the rotarod at both ages and gait abnormalities that appeared by 5.5 months, consistent with progressive motor decline.

paragraphs.text: Assoum et al. (2020) used exome sequencing to identify 2 missense variants in KIAA1033, K1079R and H503R, in a 34-year-old patient with mild intellectual disability, short stature, and microcephaly. The patient was compound heterozygous, with one variant inherited from each parent.

paragraphs.text: For discussion of the H503R variant in KIAA1033 found in compound heterozygous state in a patient with mild intellectual disability, short stature, and microcephaly, see K1079R (Assoum et al., 2020).
